articles.title: Sanctions Relief Returns Belarusian Potash to US Ports as Prices Fall - Crux Investor
articles.summary: Sanctions Relief Returns Belarusian Potash to US Ports as Prices Fall  Crux Investor
articles.full_text:
- A 30,000-tonne cargo of Belarusian muriate of potash (MOP) is scheduled to discharge at New Orleans on October 14, the first US-bound Belarusian potash in four years.
- The US Treasury delisted Belaruskali and the Belarusian Potash Company on March 26, 2026, reopening a channel that averaged 635,000 tonnes a year into the US from 2017 to 2021.
- The World Bank MOP benchmark fell from $405.00 per tonne in May 2026 to $367.50 in September, within $2.50 of its $365 forecast for 2027.
- Belarus mined 6 million tonnes of potassium oxide in 2025 against 49 million worldwide, but President Alexander Lukashenko said on September 21 that those volumes are contracted.
- A World Bank MOP price above $400 per tonne on November 3, 2026, would indicate demand absorbed returning Belarusian supply rather than displaced Canadian tonnes.
Sanctions Relief Restores Belarusian Supply to US Market
A 30,000-tonne cargo of Belarusian MOP is scheduled to discharge in New Orleans on October 14, marking the first US-bound Belarusian potash shipment in four years. The Belarusian Potash Company loaded the cargo at Russia’s port of Bronka. The World Bank MOP benchmark fell for a third consecutive month to $367.50 per tonne in September from $405.00 in May, increasing price pressure as Belarusian supply returns.
The 30,000-tonne cargo equals about 0.5% of 2025 US potash imports, limiting its immediate market impact. US potash imports reached 5.6 million tonnes of potassium oxide equivalent in 2025, with net import reliance at 92%. The larger shift is the reopening of a supply channel that carried 635,000 tonnes a year before the 2021 designations.
Lost Klaipeda Access Raises Potash Delivery Costs Through Russia
Before the 2021 designations, Lithuania’s Klaipeda terminal handled 9 million to 11 million tonnes of Belarusian potash a year. With Klaipeda closed to Belarusian cargo, shipments now move by rail through Russia to Baltic ports such as Bronka, adding transport and handling costs. Arif Gasilov, partner at Gasilov Group, said Belarus moved 11.6 million tonnes through Russian ports in 2025. Higher rail, port, insurance and handling costs reduce the competitiveness of Belarusian potash in the US, limiting the pricing threat to Canadian supply.
The Office of Foreign Assets Control issued General License 13 covering Belaruskali and the Belarusian Potash Company in December 2025 and delisted both in March 2026 after Belarus released about 250 political prisoners, reopening US trade with the companies. The EU has not matched the US relief, leaving Belarusian potash subject to EU restrictions and limiting its access to European buyers.
Committed Volumes Limit Near-Term Price Pressure
Existing sales contracts currently limit additional Belarusian potash supply to Western markets, with President Alexander Lukashenko saying Belarus has no uncommitted volumes available. Josh Linville, Vice President of Fertilizer at StoneX, noted that US buyers have had no difficulty sourcing potash, while phosphate and nitrogen remain the tighter nutrients.
Returning Supply Pressures Margins More Than Sales Volumes
For Saskatchewan-focused potash producers, returning Belarusian supply threatens realized prices more than sales volumes. Nutrien’s February 18, 2026 guidance estimates that each $25 per tonne change in potash net selling prices corresponds to $280 million of adjusted EBITDA and $0.45 of adjusted earnings per share. With tonnes already placed, additional New Orleans supply would pressure realized prices rather than displace sales volumes.
Producers with export logistics can redirect tonnes offshore, reducing exposure to weaker regional pricing. That flexibility can protect sales volumes when domestic supply increases. A pre-production developer without offtake remains exposed to benchmark prices when production begins.
No program volume or delivered price has been published, leaving the scale of Belarusian supply and its price impact uncertain, while the US Treasury retains the ability to restore sanctions. For Saskatchewan-focused producers, the key risk remains margin pressure from lower realized potash prices rather than the volume of a single cargo. For pre-production projects underwritten above $400 per tonne, a $365 benchmark can weaken projected returns and financing economics.
What Cost Position Supports Potash Returns
US sanctions restricted Belarusian potash supply, while their removal is reopening that trade channel. The World Bank MOP benchmark began falling three months before the Belarusian cargo was due, indicating the price decline preceded its return.
Since 2022, Saskatchewan-focused producers have benefited more from stronger netbacks than higher volumes, making realized pricing a key valuation driver. US Geological Survey (USGS) projects global potash capacity at 77.4 million tonnes of potassium oxide equivalent by 2029 versus 45.3 million tonnes of consumption, making delivered cost increasingly important to project economics.
Long-term value depends on delivered cost. Lower prices can delay higher-cost projects, favoring producers that remain competitive at lower potash prices. Saskatchewan producers can rail potash directly into the US Midwest, while Belarusian supply requires additional rail, port, insurance and handling costs through Russia.

articles.title: Moscow’s New Strategy toward Yerevan - The Armenian Mirror-Spectator
articles.summary: Moscow’s New Strategy toward Yerevan  The Armenian Mirror-Spectator
articles.full_text:
Alongside the pressure coming from Azerbaijan, Russia has become considerably more active in its policy towards Armenia. Most likely, recognizing that its strategic presence in the South Caucasus is under threat, Moscow changed its foreign political strategy toward Yerevan after the Armenian elections.
Russia appears to be withholding from Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan the support he had enjoyed since the 2020 war, whether through various statements by the Russian president himself or through Moscow’s political backing in helping him remain in power (as voiced by the Armenian opposition back in those days). The main objective was probably realizing the November 9, 2020, agreement, which Moscow hoped to implement as long as Pashinyan remained in power.
Today Russia has changed its strategy, and the impression is that the trust Moscow once placed in Pashinyan has taken on a different character. Moscow seeks new strategies to maintain its influence in the South Caucasus. One of its new initiatives and political moves is a project for railway and road links along the Black Sea coast connecting Russia, Georgia, and Armenia, which reportedly has been presented by Moscow. Provisionally dubbed “Putin’s Route,” the proposal has become a subject of extensive public discussion in expert circles in recent days.
Although it has not been officially announced, the public discussion is most likely a way to test the reactions of Armenia and Georgia. What is particularly interesting is that Russia is not taking this step by accident. Moscow is well aware of Pashinyan’s Crossroads of Peace initiative, and through this new proposal, it appears to be seeking a clear response from the Armenian authorities.
If Yerevan rejects Moscow’s proposal on this route, this could suggest that, from Yerevan’s perspective, the Crossroads of Peace applies only to the normalization of relations with Armenia’s direct neighbors and it would help the West to gain influence in Armenia to balance Russia. If Yerevan does not reject it, Moscow would gain an opportunity to intensify its political engagement in the South Caucasus, using this economic initiative as a basis, just like in the case of the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP).
This is a carefully calculated move that could provide answers to several important questions. It cannot be ruled out that Pashinyan and Russian President Vladimir Putin will discuss the matter at their next meeting. For Russia, whose position in the South Caucasus has weakened, every available opportunity must be used to restore its influence in what Moscow considers its traditional sphere of influence, while simultaneously counterbalancing Turkish and American influence.

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 5. Investment in transport infrastructure could help reduce the time and financial costs of regional trade with Turkmenistan and Central Asia, Iranian Deputy Minister of Economy and Finance Mehdi Heydari said.
Heydari made the remarks at the Turkmenistan Investment Forum TIF 2026 in Ashgabat, according to a press release published by the Turkmen government press service yesterday.
“Targeted investment in the modernization of railways and roads, bridges, border terminals and logistics centers on the Caspian Sea will make it possible to significantly reduce the time and financial costs of regional trade,” Heydari said.
Meanwhile, Iran and Turkmenistan have been working to increase the use of rail links connecting Central Asia with Iran and the Persian Gulf. In September 2025, the two countries discussed increasing transit cargo volumes and activating the China-Kazakhstan-Turkmenistan-Iran railway, as well as the Ashgabat Agreement corridor linking Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan and Iran with Oman. They also discussed the Armenia-Iran-Turkmenistan-Kazakhstan route.
The Uzbekistan-Turkmenistan-Iran route is another focus of regional cooperation. In June 2025, the three countries signed a protocol to develop a multimodal corridor connecting Central Asia with Europe, with measures aimed at increasing freight volumes, streamlining procedures and removing logistics barriers.
Turkmenistan's location gives Central Asian countries access to both the Caspian Sea and Iranian routes toward the Persian Gulf. Uzbekistan, for example, has been increasing the use of Turkmenistan's rail and port infrastructure, while Iran provides a southern route toward Persian Gulf markets. The development of these connections is part of wider efforts to make regional supply chains more competitive and diversify transport routes.

articles.title: Ukraine takes aim at Russia’s oil industry with frontline gains elusive - WTOV
articles.summary: Ukraine takes aim at Russia’s oil industry with frontline gains elusive  WTOV
articles.full_text:
(TNND) — Ukraine’s continued assault on Russia’s oil refineries and energy infrastructure have resulted in more than half of its refining capacity being taken offline, according to Ukrainian officials, as Kyiv hopes to choke off Moscow’s ability to fund its war effort and hinder its ability to restock its military.
The nearly five-year-old Russian invasion of Ukraine has been mired in a slog on the ground for years with limited progress in either direction, pushing the two sides to ramp up aerial onslaughts to gain an advantage.
Ukraine has made targeting Russian energy facilities a core part of its aerial onslaught in an attempt to disrupt the fuel Moscow needs to refuel its military while cutting off one of Russia’s primary sources of revenue. Despite having a much smaller military with fewer resources and advanced weapons, Ukraine has been increasingly successful at launching strikes deep inside Russia using drones.
Ukraine said recent strikes in cities deep into Russia had disabled more than half of its refining capacity, cutting off a key producer of revenue to sustain a Russian economy that has been battered by years of war and resulting sanctions. The repeated attacks on Russian energy facilities have caused significant damage, prompting the government to restrict gasoline sales at one point earlier this year.
The International Energy Agency has said some of Russia’s refineries have been targeted more than a dozen times in recent months, setting off a cycle of repeated damage and repairs that could pose long-term damage.
"We have to respond in any way (we can). With their attacks on our energy, we have to respond on their energy. First of all, oil refiners, etc.: what gives money to them for this war," Zelenskyy told Reuters. "But we will not respond, of course, just like them, on any civilian objects."
With limited manpower and a standoff on the front lines, Ukraine has increasingly tried to use long-range strikes to put costs on Russia.
“There's such a stalemate on the actual battlefield that both sides are willing to resort to more significant measures to try and find some kind of breakthrough to the conflict,” Martin said. “The temptation also with these deep strikes is that, from the Ukrainian standpoint, you can put pressure on Russia without putting your own soldiers at risk when you're already dealing with manpower challenges.”
Russia has promised to ramp up its attacks on Ukraine in response, even issuing a warning against foreign visitors and diplomats with a push to leave Kyiv. Russian attacks have increasingly targeted power plants, bridges and other civilian infrastructure in recent weeks as part of a pronounced uptick in air and drone strikes.
The Kremlin has not publicly disclosed what level of damage has been done to its oil infrastructure, but Putin recently said the attacks have cost Russia about 1% of its gross domestic product.
“They started attacking oil refineries and openly declared the goal of damaging our economy. Did they achieve their goal? Partially,” Putin said earlier this month.
The onslaught of Russian refineries comes as global energy prices are already elevated due to the war in Iran. Prior to the conflict, Russia was the third-largest producer of refined fuel products from crude oil.
The reduction in Russian fuel supplies risks putting Ukraine more at odds with the Trump administration as higher energy prices create economic and political headaches at home.
With oil prices fueling higher costs at the pump and for diesel, President Donald Trump has increasingly blamed the war in Ukraine as a driver of higher costs that are causing headaches for Republicans ahead of the November midterms. Trump asked Zelenskyy to stop attacking Russian refineries, saying they are causing a global shortage.
Energy analysts have agreed the repeated attacks on Russia’s energy sector have helped push prices higher, but they are not the sole factor that has led to diesel hitting record highs in the U.S. above $6 a gallon. A sharp drop in energy exports coming out of the Middle East due to the war with Iran and resulting closure of the Strait of Hormuz have also been a major contributor to higher energy prices.
The Trump administration has also tried to get long-stalled peace discussions restarted in recent weeks, sending White House special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv to meet with the countries’ leaders. Those preliminary discussions have yielded little progress, leaving the two sides gearing up for what is expected to be an increasingly brutal assault this winter.
Zelenskyy told Reuters over the weekend that he had received no indication Russia was ready for peace negotiations or entering a ceasefire for energy infrastructure. Last month at the United Nations, Zelenskyy had said he hoped the U.S. could help bring an end to the war before winter.
But continuing the attacks may risk Ukraine straining its relationship with an administration that has pulled back on providing aid and pushed to change course.
“There's a sense where, for the Ukrainians, they are less reliant on American aid. They're also skeptical of American mediation efforts to a degree. Their experience, especially over the last year with those 28 points that seemed to be inspired more by Russian perspectives than Ukrainian interests, I think has left a bad taste,” said Garret Martin, Hurst Senior Professorial Lecturer and the co-director of the Transatlantic Policy Center at American University. “In a way for the Ukrainians, they are probably less worried about the consequence of pursuing this course of action, even if it's not welcome for the Trump administration.”
Moscow has shown no public indications it is willing to settle the conflict or back down from its maximalist demands. Russian officials have also claimed any pause in fighting would be used for the U.S. and Europe to help Ukraine restock its military.
Analysts have said throughout the conflict that Putin’s strategy has been to wait out Ukraine’s allies’ ability to continue providing military and economic support, making the battle a war of attrition he believes favors Russia.

articles.title: SJC: Extradition of prisoners from Georgia to Russia must be stopped immediately - JAMnews
articles.summary: SJC: Extradition of prisoners from Georgia to Russia must be stopped immediately  JAMnews
articles.full_text:
Following the killing of Dmitry Pushkaryov, who Georgia extradited to Russia, the Georgian Social Justice Center (SJC) said that Georgia should immediately halt the extradition of prisoners to Russia.
The organisation said resuming the practice of extraditing prisoners to Russia was incompatible with human rights.
After Georgia extradited Dmitry Pushkaryov, he was killed in an attack on Russian Federal Penitentiary Service (FSIN) officers. According to Russian authorities, Pushkaryov killed one officer and wounded three others while attempting to escape.
“The mere fact that Dmitry Pushkaryov was killed does not directly establish that Georgia violated Article 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights by extraditing him. However, his death raises even more serious questions about how thoroughly the Georgian authorities assessed the risks he faced in Russia, what guarantees they obtained from Russia, whether an independent mechanism existed to monitor compliance with those guarantees, and whether the Georgian side subsequently monitored the person’s situation,” the SJC said.
According to the organisation, the case law of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR) indicates that information that emerges after a person’s transfer can also matter when assessing how well-founded the state’s initial risk assessment was.
The SJC believes that continuing extraditions to Russia — particularly without proper public justification, a rigorous individual risk assessment and effective independent monitoring mechanisms — could put Georgia in breach of its international human rights obligations.
The organisation calls on the Georgian government, the Ministry of Justice and the Prosecutor General’s Office to immediately suspend extraditions to Russia. The SJC believes the practice should remain suspended until the situation in Russia changes significantly and the international community reaches a consensus on the issue.
The Centre also calls on the Prosecutor General’s Office to publish statistical data on extradition requests received from Russia since 16 March 2022, the decisions made on those requests and the extraditions carried out.
The organisation is also demanding that the Ministry of Justice explain the legal grounds for changing the moratorium recorded before the European Court of Human Rights in the case of Sumbaev v. Georgia.
The ECtHR found Georgia’s 2021 extradition of Aslan Sumbaev, who faced serious criminal charges in Russia, lawful only after Russia provided official diplomatic assurances that it would prevent torture and ensure proper detention conditions.
“Please also specify what individual guarantees and subsequent monitoring mechanisms were applied in relation to the extraditions that have already taken place,” the Social Justice Center wrote.

articles.title: Kazakhstan, Oman Deepen Ties During Sultan’s First Central Asia Visit - The Astana Times
articles.summary: Kazakhstan, Oman Deepen Ties During Sultan’s First Central Asia Visit  The Astana Times
articles.full_text:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan and Oman agreed to deepen strategic partnership across energy, transport, logistics, agriculture and digitalization on Oct. 6, as Sultan Haitham bin Tariq Al Said made his first visit to Central Asia.
During the talks in Astana, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev described Oman as a “time-tested and reliable partner” of Kazakhstan in the Arab world. He noted that the two countries will mark the 35th anniversary of diplomatic relations next year.
“We have laid a solid foundation for moving to a new dynamic stage of partnership,” Tokayev said.
The two leaders also adopted a joint statement that sets out the main areas of the bilateral partnership, Akorda reported. The document reaffirms the two countries’ commitment to strengthening cooperation based on mutual respect, trust and shared interests, while outlining priorities ranging from trade and investment to transport, energy, agriculture, digital technologies, education and tourism.
Tokayev highlighted several ongoing joint projects, including the development of the Dunga oil field, Solidcore Resources’ operations in the Pavlodar and North Kazakhstan Regions, the joint investment fund with Oman Investment Authority, and projects in the hotel and resort sector.
New agreements strengthen investment and business ties
During the visit, Kazakhstan and Oman signed an intergovernmental agreement to promote and mutually protect investments, an air services agreement, an agreement establishing the Oman-Kazakhstan Business Council, and an agreement establishing a joint investment fund.
The leaders also signed an agreement setting the terms of the Eurasian Development Bank’s presence in Oman, along with several interagency memoranda covering cooperation in various fields.
The leaders agreed to diversify bilateral trade, address trade barriers and improve market access for products from both countries. They also endorsed stronger investment cooperation in energy, natural resources, manufacturing, food, healthcare, logistics, tourism, renewable energy and mining.
Transport connectivity identified as strategic priority
The joint statement highlights the strategic importance of stronger transport and logistics links between Central Asia and the Gulf region.
Kazakhstan and Oman intend to develop efficient transport corridors connecting Central Asian markets with the Gulf, the Middle East and Africa, among other key regions.
The countries also agreed to work toward launching direct, regular flights as soon as possible, saying improved air links would support business, tourism and people-to-people ties.
“We see significant opportunities for growth, investment and cooperation with Kazakhstan,” Sultan Haitham said.
Energy, digital technologies and AI
The two countries also expressed interest in joint projects in energy, petrochemicals, manufacturing and processing, while identifying agriculture and food security as promising areas for deeper cooperation.
Digital technologies, artificial intelligence, innovation and human capital development emerged as another priority. The officials will encourage partnerships between technology companies, innovation hubs and academic institutions, including through knowledge exchange and joint initiatives.
The leaders also expressed interest in expanding educational cooperation through student and academic exchanges, joint programs and collaborative research.
Sultan Haitham thanked President Tokayev for his hospitality and reaffirmed Oman’s commitment to strengthening relations with Kazakhstan. He also invited President Tokayev to visit the Sultanate of Oman.

articles.title: IRF Delegation Visits B3 Arch Bridge on Georgias North-South Corridor Road Project - ANTARA News
articles.summary: IRF Delegation Visits B3 Arch Bridge on Georgias North-South Corridor Road Project  ANTARA News
articles.full_text:
IRF Delegation Visits B3 Arch Bridge on Georgia’s North–South Corridor Road Project
The B3 Arch Bridge serves as a key controlling project for the Georgia North-South Corridor Road project. Located in a deep valley of the Caucasus Mountains, the bridge has a total length of 437.875 meters, a main arch net span of 286 meters, and a height difference of 164 meters from the bridge deck to the valley floor. It features a deck-type reinforced concrete separated twin-rib box arch structure, constructed using the cantilever casting method with cable-stayed anchoring. Subjected to extreme environmental challenges—including Beaufort scale 9 strong winds, severe cold down to -20°C, 2-meter-thick snow accumulation, and high-intensity seismic zones—the bridge, upon completion, will become the largest-span reinforced concrete arch bridge in the Caucasus region, with its span ranking among the top worldwide for similar cantilever-cast arch bridges.
During the inspection, the project team of China Railway 23rd Bureau Group delivered a detailed report to the accompanying delegates on core management measures and technical achievements.
These included the implementation of European standards, FIDIC contract management, high-precision closure control for the twin-rib main arch, intelligent monitoring, and wind tunnel test verification.
The delegation closely inspected and inquired about key structural components, such as the main arch ring construction, anchoring system, and cable hoisting system.
They engaged in in-depth exchanges with the Chinese technical team on critical topics, including main arch alignment and stress control, construction procedures, winter construction safety assurance, full-lifecycle maintenance, and follow-up construction organization.
The delegation representative stated that the North-South Corridor Road is one of the most vital transportation infrastructure projects in Georgia's national development strategy, playing a decisive role in strengthening the country's status as an Eurasian transit hub.
As the most technically challenging controlling project along the entire route, the B3 Arch Bridge fully demonstrates the capability of Chinese enterprises in building large-scale bridges under complex geological and extreme climatic conditions.
Strictly adhering to European technical specifications and the FIDIC management system, the project meets world-class standards in quality control, environmental protection, and localized employment, setting a new benchmark for highway and bridge construction in Georgia and across the broader Central Asia–Caucasus region.

Han Shuai, project manager of the China Railway 23rd Bureau Co., Ltd. North–South Corridor Road Project, said that the company would take this visit by the IRF delegation as an opportunity to continue pursuing its overseas business philosophy of "Quality Delivery, Safety First, Standards Alignment and Local Integration." The project team will make every effort to achieve key milestones, including the closure of the B3 main arch in 2026, and develop the project into a model of infrastructure cooperation between China and Georgia and a landmark project for bridge construction in high-altitude mountainous regions under the Belt and Road Initiative.
As a vivid embodiment of the theme of this year's IRF Congress—"Resilient, Intelligent and Safe Roads Driving Sustainable Growth"—the site visit to the B3 Arch Bridge brought delegates from conference halls to the front lines of project construction, transforming conceptual discussions into first-hand evidence from an actual engineering project. The bridge spans not only the deep valleys of the Caucasus, but also represents a new level of mutual trust and cooperation between China, Europe and Central Asia in the field of transportation infrastructure.

articles.title: Russia's Fuel Subsidies Hit Highest Since 2022 - Briefs Finance
articles.summary: Russia's Fuel Subsidies Hit Highest Since 2022  Briefs Finance
articles.full_text:
What happened
According to Russia's Finance Ministry, oil companies received 305.5 billion rubles in September to bolster domestic road-fuel supply, an amount exceeded only in April 2022. Since January, the running total of these payouts has climbed past $14 billion. Those September subsidies were just shy of the 323.3 billion rubles the oil sector paid into the federal budget that month. Interfax reported, citing documents sent to the State Duma with the 2027-29 budget draft, that the government projects the subsidy bill to reach 1.93 trillion rubles for all of 2026 and to drop to 1.18 trillion rubles the year after.
Why the payments rose
Ukraine has been hitting a wide range of Russian oil infrastructure - pipeline links, export terminals, and refineries - in a bid to curb the money backing the Kremlin's war, now in its fifth year. The strikes have reduced output of oil products, triggering gasoline shortages, rationing, and queues at forecourts. Producers have had to undertake broad unplanned maintenance, and some plants cut runs or shut down entirely after the attacks. The subsidies are helping keep refiners afloat through that disruption.
Wartime strikes on refineries reach drivers long before they reach headlines. Market Briefs tracks fuel markets free every morning.
How the subsidies work and who gets them
The formula links subsidies to refiners' domestic sales volumes and to the differential between wholesale prices at home and on the export market. To keep plants running, subsidies continue despite restrictions on overseas sales, including a prohibition covering the bulk of gasoline, diesel, and jet-fuel exports. Another rule halting diesel exports remains in effect through the end of October.
Most of the funding is directed to the biggest oil producers - such as Rosneft PJSC and Tatneft PJSC - that run the country's key refineries. To keep domestic supply steady, the government has also opened the door for fuel importers to receive support.
There is a quirk in the mechanism: when the regulated base price for car fuel at home rises above export pricing, refiners actually pay into the budget, which shows up as negative subsidies. There were no such payments in October 2023.
Budget impact and what it means for your portfolio
Based on Finance Ministry data, Bloomberg calculates that Russia's net oil and gas income in September totaled 452.4 billion rubles, a drop of more than one fifth from a year earlier. That happened even with Urals crude priced higher than last year and a weaker ruble. The ministry's oil revenue tally folds in the extraction tax on gas condensate, the profit based tax, and refinery subsidies, and the hefty September payouts were a big reason net income fell.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told Reuters over the weekend that Kyiv will intensify strikes on Russian energy facilities after sustained attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. For your wallet, the simple read is that Russia is diverting more cash to keep domestic fuel flowing, which reshapes how much budget money is left over and how reliably oil-and-gas cash flows through its economy.

articles.title: Tokayev shapes Kazakhstan’s technological future: AI & Digital Bridge highlights - Trend News Agency
articles.summary: Tokayev shapes Kazakhstan’s technological future: AI & Digital Bridge highlights  Trend News Agency
articles.full_text:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 5. President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev places particular emphasis on the development of artificial intelligence and digital technologies. In this context, he declared 2026 the Year of Digitalization and Artificial Intelligence, while a dedicated Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development was established in 2025. The AI & Digital Bridge 2026 international forum, held in Astana from October 1 to 3, emerged as one of the major events of the year in this field.
According to Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov, more than 60 new contracts were signed during the forum. Although many of these remain memorandums of intent, they nevertheless indicate the key directions in which the government seeks to advance Kazakhstan’s digital sector.
A memorandum on cooperation in the development of the digital assets market and the application of blockchain technologies in Kazakhstan was signed between the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development of Kazakhstan and Kraken. KASE and the administration of Alatau City reached an agreement on cooperation in the field of digital financial assets. Astana Hub and Uzbekistan’s IT Park signed a memorandum aimed at facilitating the entry of startups from the two countries into international markets. The Ministry of Energy signed three documents with Chinese partners covering joint developments in energy, artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure. In addition, an agreement was reached with the GSMA association to hold the M360 Eurasia forum in Astana in autumn 2027.
At the opening of the forum, Tokayev proposed compiling a list of industrial challenges for AI based on the actual needs of the economy and launching an AI Challenge for Kazakh and international teams on this basis. He also cautioned that excessive regulation could encourage promising teams and capital to move to other jurisdictions.
The following day, during a meeting of the Council for the Development of Artificial Intelligence, the president set the task of moving from individual digital solutions to the systematic use of AI in industry. He referred to the United Nations Industrial Development Organization's 2026 report: over five years, the share of patents related to AI has increased approximately threefold, while competition is also taking place over the pace of improving production efficiency.
Such an approach also requires appropriate infrastructure. If AI is to be used in enterprises, energy, and transport, Kazakhstan needs its own large-scale computing capacity. For this purpose, the "Data Center Valley" is being created in Ekibastuz - the largest data center in Central Asia, with capacity expected to reach 1 GW in the long term.
The first stage of the project is estimated at $5 billion, of which $1 billion will be invested by Kazakhtelecom. At this stage, around 100,000 next-generation GPUs are planned to be deployed. The main buildings and energy infrastructure are expected to be completed by the end of December 2026.
Kazakhstan is effectively using its advantages - access to energy, a large territory, and its location between major markets. The country does not produce advanced chips itself, but is focusing on creating infrastructure for their use.
Ekibastuz, one of the country's largest coal and energy centers, was selected for the project based on its available energy base.
The authorities estimate the project's potential export revenue at $3 billion per year. However, actual figures will depend on demand for computing capacity, which may change along with the global technology market.
To attract foreign clients, Astana is also working on the legal framework. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development Zhaslan Madiyev said the government is developing a "data embassies" regime under which major technology companies will be able to operate under a separate international legal framework. Under the concept, foreign states will be able to store data in Kazakhstan while retaining full legal sovereignty over it.
Kazakhstan's task is not only to create large data centers, but also to generate demand for their capacity. If the country can attract foreign clients while ensuring broad use of AI across the domestic economy, Kazakhstan's energy and infrastructure advantages could provide a basis for developing a new area of digital services.
This was also discussed at AI & Digital Bridge 2026. The forum presented projects in energy, industry, transport and finance where AI is already planned for practical use. Kazakhstan now needs to bring these projects to implementation and ensure real demand for them. This would allow the infrastructure being created to support not only the development of the digital sector, but also the economy as a whole.

Investment cooperation

Financial partnership

Energy and mining

Transport and agriculture

Kazakhstan, he said, brings extensive natural resources, an established industrial base and a strategic position along emerging transport routes connecting Asia and Europe, alongside plans to further strengthen connectivity.

From agreements to projects

articles.title: BRI connectivity: What next for HK legal profession’s role? - chinadailyhk
articles.summary: BRI connectivity: What next for HK legal profession’s role?  chinadailyhk
articles.full_text:
Thomas So says city can strengthen its position as a trusted bridge by helping build legal corridors that complement the physical corridors
As the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) enters a new phase of high-quality development that pivots heavily toward renewable energy, high-tech industrial manufacturing and telecommunications infrastructure, legal services are playing an increasingly important role in facilitating cross-border trade, investment and regional cooperation. While infrastructure and finance remain key drivers of connectivity, sustainable economic partnerships ultimately rely on legal certainty, trusted institutions and effective dispute-resolution mechanisms.
The Law Society of Hong Kong, the statutory self-regulatory body of solicitors in Hong Kong, established a dedicated Belt and Road Committee to deepen engagement with BRI-participating jurisdictions and strengthen professional exchanges and collaboration in 2015. It has continued to hold an annual Belt and Road Law Conference since 2017, with the latest edition, held on Sept 10, focusing on the growing importance of Central Asia within the BRI framework, and examining how legal innovation can support trade, investment and professional cooperation across the region.
The conference brought together legal experts from around the world to discuss ways in which legal infrastructure in various jurisdictions could further facilitate commercial activities and investment flows across BRI-participating economies. There was also a discussion on the growing importance of mediation, arbitration and litigation working together to deliver practical and commercially effective solutions for parties operating across different jurisdictions.
The evolving role of Hong Kong’s legal profession
As BRI projects become increasingly sophisticated, legal practitioners must possess a broader understanding of commercial realities, financing structures, regulatory requirements, and cross-cultural business practices. Legal services have become an integral part of the investment lifecycle, helping businesses identify opportunities, manage risks, and navigate complex international transactions.
This is particularly relevant in light of the national 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30), which supports Hong Kong’s development as an international legal and dispute-resolution services center in the Asia-Pacific region. To continue fulfilling this role, Hong Kong's legal profession must continue to evolve alongside the changing needs of international commerce.
Supporting Hong Kong’s role in national strategy
To reinforce Hong Kong’s position as an international legal services center, the legal profession should continue to deepen expertise in areas increasingly relevant to BRI cooperation, including cross-border investment, infrastructure development, project finance, energy transition, digital trade, and regulatory compliance.
Talent development must remain a strategic priority. More specialized training should be provided to equip legal practitioners with a deeper understanding of BRI-participating jurisdictions, particularly emerging markets such as Central Asia. Exchanges with overseas lawyers’ associations, legal institutions and professional bodies can further strengthen professional capabilities and foster long-term partnerships. Hong Kong can also contribute to the cultivation of international legal talent by serving as a platform where legal professionals from different jurisdictions learn, collaborate, and develop mutual understanding.
Hong Kong’s legal profession also plays an important role in supporting Chinese-mainland enterprises seeking to expand internationally. As more mainland businesses “go global”, demand is growing for legal services relating to investment structuring, risk management, compliance, and market entry. Hong Kong lawyers are uniquely positioned to provide practical support throughout the investment lifecycle, helping businesses navigate unfamiliar legal environments and manage cross-border risks.
Looking ahead
As the BRI continues to evolve, legal connectivity will become increasingly important alongside physical and digital connectivity. Leveraging its unique strengths as the world’s only bilingual English-Chinese common law jurisdiction, Hong Kong is well positioned to fulfill its role as an international legal and dispute-resolution services center.
To remain at the forefront, the legal profession must continue evolving with the changing needs of international commerce by deepening specialized expertise, nurturing international legal talent, supporting the work of the International Organization for Mediation, enhancing dispute resolution services, and assisting mainland enterprises in their global expansion.
The legal profession in Hong Kong must continue with its promotion of professional excellence and international legal cooperation. By helping build the legal corridors that complement the BRI's physical corridors, Hong Kong can further strengthen its role as a trusted legal bridge connecting the mainland, BRI-participating jurisdictions, and other parts of the world, contributing to regional prosperity and high-quality international cooperation.
The author is chair of the Belt and Road Committee of the Law Society of Hong Kong, and a member of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference and the Legislative Council of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region.
The views do not necessarily reflect those of China Daily.

articles.title: IRGC commander, son helped build new oil-sales network - Iran International
articles.summary: IRGC commander, son helped build new oil-sales network  Iran International
articles.full_text:
Senior IRGC commander Hossein-Reza Sadeghi and his son Saeed played central roles in efforts to preserve an IRGC Intelligence oil-sales network and shift its financial operations from the United Arab Emirates to Russia, an Iran International investigation found.
Two informed sources told Iran International that Sadeghi, a senior adviser to the Revolutionary Guards commander-in-chief, and his son were at the center of efforts to shift the mechanism for transferring sanctioned oil revenues from the UAE to Russia.
The sources linked the changes to the departure of Oil Minister Mohsen Paknejad.
On Sunday, the IRGC-affiliated Fars news agency reported that Iran’s Central Bank had found an alternative route to repatriate money held by oil intermediaries trusted by the Islamic Republic, known as “trustees,” and transferred $1.5 billion in Iranian oil revenues through Russia’s banking system.
Hours after the report, Paknejad resigned and President Masoud Pezeshkian accepted his resignation.
The two sources said Paknejad’s removal and the change in the money-transfer route were part of an effort to preserve the IRGC Intelligence Organization’s oil-sales corruption network.
Saeed Sadeghi’s role in Iran’s oil sector
Although Saeed Sadeghi currently holds no official Oil Ministry position, he has for years been a trusted Revolutionary Guards figure in Iran’s oil industry.
During Ebrahim Raisi’s presidency, he became chief executive of Amir Kabir Petrochemical Company. He previously served as deputy for legal affairs and contracts at the oil, gas and petrochemical holding company of the Guards’ Khatam al-Anbiya Construction Headquarters and at Shastan Investment Holding, which is affiliated with the Defense Ministry.
Two months after Pezeshkian took office, Sadeghi was appointed chief executive of Naftiran Intertrade Company (NICO). In September 2025, he was removed just one week after being appointed director of international affairs at the National Iranian Oil Company.
His removal came after it emerged that trustees had failed to return $8 billion in proceeds from oil sales to Iran.
After anti-government protests broke out in January, several establishment figures said economic pressure stemming from corruption among the trustees had caused the unrest.
Mehdi Kharatian, director of the Hayat-e Siasat think tank and an analyst close to the Islamic Republic, compared “the trustees’ failure to return the dollars” to “the pager operation in Iran” during a video podcast.
Iran International’s sources said Sadeghi traveled to Moscow at his father’s request a week before the start of the 40-day war, apparently to avoid possible judicial proceedings.
He remained in Russia until the war ended and worked on moving the financial network used to handle proceeds from sanctioned Iranian oil sales from the UAE to Russia, the sources said.
Shift from UAE to Russia
On June 6, Mohammad Javad Bavand, a former deputy head of the IRGC Intelligence Organization’s economic affairs division, was appointed the oil minister’s special assistant for sales.
Bavand had held the same position under Raisi and previously represented IRGC Intelligence on the Supreme National Security Council committee tasked with circumventing sanctions.
On June 17, Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati visited Mir Business Bank in Moscow alongside Iran’s ambassador to Russia.
Bank Melli Iran owns all shares in the bank, which is registered in Moscow and has operated since 2002. Mir Business Bank provides correspondent accounts and services for ruble and foreign-currency transactions, connecting Iranian banks with Russia’s banking network.
The US Treasury sanctioned the bank in 2018 for providing financial services to sanctioned Iranian entities.
Iran International’s sources said proceeds from oil sold by the trustees are to be returned to Iran through Russia’s Mir financial network, which they said replaced SWIFT following US banking sanctions.
IRGC Intelligence builds new network
IRGC Brigadier General Hossein-Reza Sadeghi was tasked with completing the IRGC Intelligence Organization’s network for selling Iranian oil, according to Iran International’s sources.
Sadeghi has held senior oversight positions within the Revolutionary Guards, including heading the office responsible for special oversight of IRGC Intelligence on behalf of the Guards’ commander-in-chief. He has also served as deputy coordinator of the IRGC Intelligence Protection Organization.
The sources said the establishment of the IRGC trustee network was approved by Mehdi Sayyari, the new acting head of the IRGC Intelligence Organization.
At the same time, a separate network of oil intermediaries linked to Iran’s Intelligence Ministry, known as Shayan, came under scrutiny by the ministry’s internal security unit. Shayan, the ministry’s director-general for fuel and energy, was subsequently removed from his post.
Previous investigations traced billions in oil proceeds
One week later, Iran International identified nine trustees in the network, including children of senior security figures, among them Ali Rezaei, son of Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei.
Members of the network have collectively failed to return $11 billion in proceeds from Iranian oil sales, Iran International’s investigation found.
Two weeks later, Iran International published two confidential documents showing that Mohammad Javad Bavand, an IRGC-linked official in the Oil Ministry, had assigned the sale of 86 million barrels of Iranian oil to four trustees who already owed money from previous sales.
Iran International’s sources said that after the reports were published, IRGC commander Abdollah Zeighami, also known as Moshfegh and deputy head of the Revolutionary Guards’ media headquarters, held a confidential meeting with Bavand and Mostafa Ahadi, a former deputy for economic affairs at IRGC Intelligence who now serves as deputy head of Unit 600 of the IRGC Intelligence Organization.
The sources said the meeting focused on suppressing reporting about corruption involving IRGC-linked oil trustees.
Iran International’s sources said Sunday’s transfer of $1.5 billion in oil proceeds from Russia to Iran marked the completion of the Revolutionary Guards’ project.
Paknejad resigned hours later.
The sources said Paknejad had himself played a central role in establishing oil-sales corruption networks involving two of the Islamic Republic’s security agencies. He was removed after the new IRGC Intelligence network had been completed, while all the trustees remained free.

articles.title: Russia ramps up attacks on Kyiv infrastructure as U.S. makes fresh push for peace talks - CNBC
articles.summary: Russia ramps up attacks on Kyiv infrastructure as U.S. makes fresh push for peace talks  CNBC
articles.full_text:
Russia’s Defense Ministry has pledged to further intensify military attacks on Kyiv and other major Ukrainian cities, following strikes on a second major bridge in Ukraine’s capital over the weekend.
The latest threat comes as Russian forces have ramped up attacks on Kyiv in recent weeks, targeting data centers, telecommunications facilities and energy infrastructure as it seeks to disrupt daily life in the capital and force power cuts ahead of winter.
A Russian drone struck Kyiv’s key Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River on Saturday, damaging the road surface and forcing traffic to be suspended. Two people were injured in the attack, according to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko.
The attack came shortly after German Chancellor Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv to pledge 1 billion euros ($1.1 billion) in military aid to Ukraine, and after Russian drones repeatedly targeted Kyiv’s Southern Bridge earlier in the week.
In an update posted via Telegram on Sunday, Russia’s Defense Ministry confirmed the attack on the Northern Bridge, saying the bridge “supports the transfer of troops and the logistics of military cargo.”
The ministry also responded to comments from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
In an interview with Reuters, Zelenskyy said in comments published Saturday that Ukraine would double down on attacking Russian oil refineries in retaliation to a new policy of airstrikes designed to force people to abandon Kyiv and other cities. Ukraine’s president said Russian civilians would not be targeted in these strikes.
“In response to these threats, the Russian Defence Ministry recalls that the massive strikes are launched against Kiev and other Ukrainian regions specifically in retaliation for the actions of the Kiev regime’s leader,” Russia’s Defense Ministry said Sunday via Telegram, according to a Google translation.
Zelenskyy “bears full personal and political responsibility” for these intensified strikes, the ministry said.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine more than four-and-a-half years ago, with fighting along the frontline virtually deadlocked as the conflict continues into a fifth winter.
Zelenskyy said via social media on Sunday that the Trump administration has proposed a trilateral meeting at the technical level by the end of October, adding that Ukraine is open to the United Arab Emirates or another country proposed by the American side hosting the talks.
“I know they will propose this to the Russian side as well, or may have already done so. We will wait for the response. We respond positively to negotiations,” Zelenskyy said.
CNBC has contacted a spokesperson for the White House and Russia’s Embassy in London and is awaiting a response.
U.S. President Donald Trump has previously urged Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks are “hurting the world” as fuel supply disruptions continue to prop up U.S. diesel prices.

articles.title: Real risks or empty threats? Reaction to Medvedev's statement about 'Ukrainisation' of Armenia - JAMnews
articles.summary: Real risks or empty threats? Reaction to Medvedev's statement about 'Ukrainisation' of Armenia  JAMnews
articles.full_text:
Medvedev on the “Ukrainisation” of Armenia
“Armenia turning into a new Ukraine represents another sign of Russia’s geopolitical anxiety and the deepening crisis in Armenian-Russian relations,” political analyst Ruben Mehrabyan said in response to Dmitry Medvedev’s sensational statement.
“Armenia’s current leadership decided that changing the country’s course would serve its interests. I am sure that this will not lead to anything good either. The worst thing that could happen to Armenia is for it to turn into a new Ukraine,” said Russia’s deputy Security Council chairman.
By a change in course, he meant Armenia’s drive towards European integration. Yerevan has not officially responded to his remarks.
Only parliament speaker Ruben Rubinyan told journalists: “Armenia cannot be anything else. Armenia is Armenia, and it will always be Armenia.”
Political analyst Ruben Mehrabyan believes that Russia “is irritated and unbalanced because the situation in the war is not just bad, but very bad”. At the same time, the analyst says Armenia should take the statement from Moscow seriously and try to assess how real the threat is:
“We should not treat this threat as either an absolutely inevitable scenario or empty bravado. It involves real risks stemming from Armenia’s energy and economic vulnerabilities. It also contains elements of psychological pressure.”

- What Pashinyan and Putin agreed in Bishkek amid peak tensions in relations
- ‘If Russia decides to withdraw its military base, we will not object’ – Pashinyan
Comment
Political analyst Ruben Mehrabyan says Russia fears losing its influence in the South Caucasus:
“Against the backdrop of setbacks on the Ukrainian front, Moscow’s resources remain limited, while its influence across the post-Soviet space has weakened. But the most unwelcome development for Russia is that all of this now shows a clear trend towards further deterioration.”
In his view, Russia can still wage a war of attrition in Ukraine, but casualties, economic sanctions and international isolation are creating significant tensions inside the country.
The analyst says that under these conditions, Russia sees the departure of any ally as a “stab in the back”. This leads to an unbalanced response, as Medvedev’s statement demonstrates:
“The aim of the threat is to instil fear in Armenian society and stop the process of rapprochement with the West, which stems from our security and development interests.”
Mehrabyan believes the threats from Moscow carry some real risks:
“The possibility of a direct military invasion is currently close to zero for one simple reason. No matter how many threats Medvedev spews, Russia has no way to invade a country with which it has no border. But Russia has powerful hybrid tools, and it can and does use them.”
Among the existing risks, the political analyst highlights Armenia’s economic and energy dependence on Russia.
He points to the Upper Lars checkpoint, the only land route linking Armenia with Russia. Whenever the route closes, it creates problems for Armenian exporters and importers. Mehrabyan also notes that Armenia receives gas from Russia, as well as fuel for its nuclear power plant:
“Cutting off gas supplies or suspending deliveries under the pretext of repairs, or closing the border on sanitary grounds, could trigger internal upheaval in Armenia and force the country to operate under a state of emergency.”
According to Mehrabyan, Yerevan has so far managed the potential risks without shocks or conflicts, but he is not confident that it will continue to do so.
He stresses that the current situation also creates potential security risks. In particular, he suggests that “Baku could sell its pressure on Armenia to Moscow”, and that Russia would have no objection to such a deal.
The political analyst says Russia is behaving like a wounded beast. He urges the Armenian authorities to summon the Russian ambassador to the Foreign Ministry and hand him a formal protest note instead of making public demarches.
At the same time, he says Armenia needs to emphasise once again that its closer ties with the European Union and the United States serve Armenia’s interests and do not target Russia.
Mehrabyan identifies energy and economic diversification among Yerevan’s priorities. He says Armenia urgently needs to secure gas supplies from Iran, which could cover 85% of the country’s needs. He also expects the authorities to:
- continue army reforms and work to strengthen the country’s borders;
- deepen military and technical cooperation with various countries, including France, India and Greece;
- ensure domestic stability and resilience;
- strengthen strategic communications and combat disinformation.
Ruben Mehrabyan believes Armenia needs to prepare for modern warfare, including hybrid attacks:
“Armenia must not give Azerbaijan or Russia any reason to be tempted to commit aggression against us.”

articles.summary: New era of cooperation takes shape between Oman and Kazakhstan  Muscat Daily
articles.full_text:
Astana, Kazakhstan – The Sultanate of Oman and the Republic of Kazakhstan have agreed to deepen their strategic partnership, with focus on expanding bilateral trade, boosting investment, strengthening connectivity and developing cooperation in emerging sectors.
The commitments were outlined in a joint statement issued following the state visit of His Majesty Sultan Haitham bin Tarik to Kazakhstan on October 5 and 6, 2026, at the invitation of President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev.
The visit marked a historic milestone as the first state visit by the Sultan of Oman to Kazakhstan, underscoring the growing relations between the two countries.
The two leaders held high-level talks on bilateral relations, ongoing joint projects and opportunities to further intensify cooperation. They also exchanged views on regional and international developments and reaffirmed their commitment to relations based on mutual respect, trust and constructive cooperation.
A key priority identified in the joint statement was expanding bilateral trade and diversifying the range of goods exchanged between the two countries.
Oman and Kazakhstan agreed to take coordinated measures to broaden trade, address existing barriers and facilitate greater access for products from both countries to their respective markets.
The leaders also stressed the importance of expanding investment cooperation in energy, natural resources, manufacturing, food, healthcare, logistics, tourism, renewable energy and mining.
They highlighted the potential for increased mutual investment and joint economic initiatives that could create new production capacities, generate employment and strengthen industrial cooperation.
The two sides also called for stronger business partnerships between the Astana International Financial Centre and Oman International Financial Centre.
Several key agreements were signed during the visit, including an agreement on the reciprocal encouragement and protection of investment, an air transport agreement and another establishing a joint investment fund.
Other agreements covered the establishment of a presence for the Eurasian Development Bank in Oman and the creation of the Oman-Kazakhstan Business Council, alongside a number of interagency memoranda of understanding.
Connectivity and energy
The leaders placed particular emphasis on strengthening transport and logistics connectivity between Central Asia and the Gulf, highlighting the potential of Oman and Kazakhstan to contribute to sustainable corridors linking Central Asian markets with the Middle East, Africa and other regions.
They also stressed the importance of establishing direct and regular air connectivity between Oman and Kazakhstan, which would support business, tourism, cultural exchanges and people-to-people contacts.
Agriculture and food security were identified as further areas with significant potential for cooperation.
In the energy sector, the two countries reaffirmed their interest in deeper cooperation and expressed readiness to explore mutually beneficial joint projects in energy, petrochemicals, industrial production and processing.
Digital technology and education
The partnership will also extend into future-oriented sectors, with both sides highlighting opportunities in digital technologies, artificial intelligence, innovation and human capital development.
The two countries expressed readiness to encourage partnerships between technology companies, innovation hubs and academic institutions to promote knowledge exchange and innovation.
Education and research will also receive greater attention through student and academic staff exchanges, joint educational programmes and collaborative research initiatives.
The leaders reaffirmed the important role of the Oman-Kazakhstan Joint Committee in broadening cooperation and agreed to maintain regular political dialogue and communication at the highest levels.
At the conclusion of the visit, President Tokayev expressed appreciation to His Majesty for the state visit, while His Majesty Sultan Haitham thanked the Kazakh President for the warm hospitality extended to him and his delegation.
His Majesty reaffirmed Oman’s commitment to strengthening friendly and mutually beneficial relations with Kazakhstan and extended an invitation to President Tokayev to visit the sultanate.

articles.title: Grandall opens offices in Los Angeles and Almaty, Kazakhstan - Law.asia
articles.summary: Grandall opens offices in Los Angeles and Almaty, Kazakhstan  Law.asia

Grandall Law Firm has opened offices in Los Angeles in the US and Almaty in Kazakhstan, further expanding its global footprint to 42 offices worldwide.
The firm had previously established offices in New York in the US and Tashkent in Uzbekistan, Central Asia.
Li Chun, founding and executive partner of Grandall, told China Business Law Journal that the Los Angeles and Almaty offices “represent two key parts of the firm’s global service network, covering a ‘mature market’ and an ‘emerging market’, respectively”, with the aim of “helping Chinese companies ‘go further with greater stability’”.
“Grandall’s return to the US west coast signals that large Chinese law firms are beginning to reassess the opportunities and scope for co-operation between the US capital markets, and the technology sector and China. Kazakhstan, at the heart of Central Asia, is a key hub for the Belt and Road Initiative and China’s westward development,” he said.
Managing partner Li Shuang, formerly a partner at the firm’s Tianjin office, will move to the US to head the office in Los Angeles.
Li Shuang has expertise in US capital markets and cross-border legal services for companies. She has led teams advising on Nasdaq and NYSE IPOs, follow-on offerings and cross-border M&A involving listed companies. She also has substantial experience in cross-border capital transactions and Chinese companies’ overseas expansion.
The office advises on investment structures, company formation, commercial contracts, employment, data and export-control compliance and dispute resolution, as well as immigration planning and other cross-border legal services.
Grandall said in a press release that its New York and Los Angeles offices would work together to “provide Chinese companies entering and establishing themselves in the US and expanding into global markets with legal support covering multiple stages and scenarios”.
The Almaty office is headed by Wen Xiaojun, formerly head and managing partner of Grandall’s Urumqi office. He will divide his time between Urumqi and Almaty.
Wen focuses on capital markets, including domestic listings, enterprise bonds, corporate bonds and other debt instruments. He has also conducted specialised compliance reviews for various large companies.
The office’s practice spans cross-border investment and M&A, energy and infrastructure, international finance and cross-border compliance and regulation. Its services cover the full investment lifecycle, from pre-investment risk assessment and project implementation to ongoing operational compliance, while balancing compliance risk management with commercial development.
Kazakhstan, in Central Asia, is the world’s largest landlocked country, while Almaty is its largest city. The new office is at 6 Zataevich Street in the city’s central Medeu district.
Grandall said establishing a presence in Kazakhstan was “an important step in the firm’s international strategy” and would “help Chinese companies resolve complex cross-border compliance issues and strengthen their defences against legal risks”.

articles.full_text:
The government of Uzbekistan and the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) have officially signed a comprehensive partnership program spanning from 2026 to 2030, aiming to implement 15 strategic development projects across the Central Asian nation. The agreement was formalized during a high-level meeting in Tashkent on October 5, 2026, marking a significant deepening of bilateral economic ties. The extensive framework focuses heavily on modernizing public infrastructure, enhancing industrial energy efficiency, and fostering robust private-sector growth.
Mechanisms of the New Investment Framework
The strategic partnership was ratified by Uzbekistan's Minister of Investment, Industry and Trade, Laziz Kudratov, alongside Katsura Miyazaki, the Senior Vice President of JICA. The agreed framework outlines a structured deployment of Japanese Official Development Assistance (ODA) loans, technical cooperation grants, and direct private-sector investment financing. A central component of the new agenda involves the targeted development of free economic zones (FEZs) throughout Uzbekistan.
To facilitate this industrial expansion, JICA has committed to providing specialized technical assistance for drafting master plans for these economic zones. The initiative is specifically engineered to optimize the regulatory and physical environments necessary to attract substantial foreign direct investment, with a pronounced emphasis on integrating Japanese corporate enterprises into the Uzbek market. The structured funding mechanisms are designed to bypass traditional bureaucratic bottlenecks, delivering capital directly to participating financial institutions for downstream lending.
Comparison with Previous Development Cycles
JICA has maintained a continuous presence in Uzbekistan since 1993, historically concentrating its resources on foundational public works, basic healthcare access, and agricultural diversification. However, the 2026–2030 program demonstrates a marked evolution in strategic priorities. While previous portfolios included localized livestock support and the procurement of basic medical diagnostic equipment, the current agenda shifts aggressively towards macroeconomic structural reform and green energy transitions.
Earlier in 2026, JICA established the precedent for this new direction by signing extensive ODA loan agreements specifically aimed at promoting energy efficiency in both industrial facilities and public buildings. This transition reflects Uzbekistan’s broader national pivot towards a green economy, prioritizing the reduction of industrial carbon footprints and the reinforcement of national energy security over traditional, resource-heavy industrial expansion.
Accountability and Implementation Benchmarks
The successful execution of the 15 projects will require rigorous oversight and inter-ministerial coordination. The Uzbek government has assumed the primary responsibility for ensuring that the allocated funds directly stimulate the intended sectors without administrative friction. During previous diplomatic engagements in Tokyo, Uzbek Foreign Minister Bakhtiyor Saidov and JICA President Akihiko Tanaka established preliminary agreements that laid the groundwork for this accelerated project rollout.
The implementation of the energy efficiency projects, for instance, involves a two-step loan process managed by the National Agency for Energy Efficiency. This structure dictates that the primary funds are distributed to local financial institutions, which bear the ultimate accountability for selecting viable industrial borrowers and ensuring that the capital is exclusively utilized for purchasing and installing certified energy-efficient equipment. The repayment period for these infrastructural loans extends to 25 years, incorporating a seven-year grace period to allow for genuine economic stabilization before debt servicing commences.
Human Distribution and Socioeconomic Impacts
The socioeconomic distribution of these investments is projected to be far-reaching. By targeting healthcare infrastructure and human capital development, the partnership aims to directly improve the quality of life for the general Uzbek population. The modernization of transport networks and energy grids is expected to mitigate frequent power disruptions that historically hindered local enterprise and domestic life in rural areas.
Furthermore, the focus on private-sector support is designed to cultivate a new generation of entrepreneurs, particularly youth and women-led micro, small, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs). Financial inclusion projects embedded within the broader JICA agenda seek to provide these marginalized commercial demographics with unprecedented access to competitive credit, thereby decentralizing economic opportunity away from state-owned monoliths and towards grassroots commercial innovation.
Strategic Alternatives and Regional Connectivity
While the Japanese partnership is a cornerstone of Uzbekistan's development strategy, the nation is concurrently navigating a complex geopolitical landscape, actively pursuing connectivity and investment from diverse international corridors. The JICA framework competes and synergizes with investments from European development banks and neighboring economic powers.
| Key Dimensions of the 2026–2030 Uzbekistan-JICA Partnership |  |  | 
|---|---|---|
| Sector Focus | Strategic Objective | Primary Mechanism | 
|---|---|---|
| Free Economic Zones | Attract foreign investment, notably Japanese firms | Master plan technical assistance | 
| Energy Infrastructure | Transition to green economy and mitigate climate change | Two-step ODA loans to local banks | 
| Private Sector Support | Empower MSMEs and foster industrial diversification | Private Sector Investment Finance | 
| Human Capital | Upgrade education and healthcare basic needs | Technical cooperation and grants | 
The definitive success of the 15 projects will heavily depend on Uzbekistan’s capacity to maintain internal economic stability and implement the structural reforms required by international financial institutions. As the initial projects commence deployment, international observers will monitor the tangible outcomes of this ambitious, multi-billion-yen modernization effort.

articles.summary: Germany to host Central Asian leaders in Berlin for strategic Z5+1 summit  https://streamlinefeed.co.ke/
articles.full_text:
Germany is preparing to host the heads of state from five Central Asian nations in Berlin, elevating the "Z5+1" diplomatic format as Europe intensifies its push to secure critical minerals and alternative energy corridors from the resource-rich region. The summit will bring together the leaders of Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan with German Chancellor Olaf Scholz, highlighting a mutual desire to diversify economic ties and reduce historical reliance on Russia and China amid shifting global supply chains.
The Berlin Agenda: Critical Minerals and Connectivity
The primary focus of the Berlin summit is the securing of raw materials essential for Europe's green transition. Central Asia holds vast, largely untapped reserves of uranium, rare earth elements, copper, and lithium—commodities that the European Union has designated as critical for its domestic manufacturing base. Germany, as Europe's largest industrial economy, is particularly eager to establish direct, sanction-compliant supply chains that bypass traditional transit routes through Russia.
German Ambassador to Turkmenistan Petra Dachtler confirmed the upcoming high-level talks, emphasizing the strategic importance of the "Middle Corridor," also known as the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route. This multimodal network connects Central Asia to Europe via the Caspian Sea, Azerbaijan, and the Black Sea, offering a vital logistical alternative to the sanctioned Northern Corridor. The Berlin summit aims to secure German engineering and financial backing to expand the capacity of this corridor, which currently suffers from severe bottlenecks and maritime transshipment delays.
Europe's Multi-Vector Courtship
The "Z5+1" format—referring to the five Central Asian republics plus one external partner—has become a primary diplomatic tool for global powers seeking influence in the region. While the United States, Japan, and South Korea regularly hold their own C5+1 summits, Germany's decision to host the heads of state directly in Berlin signals a significant upgrade in European engagement. The European Union's Global Gateway initiative has pledged billions in infrastructure investments to the region, focusing on digital connectivity, water diplomacy, and sustainable energy projects.
For Germany, the stakes are heavily tied to its industrial sector. Companies like BASF and Siemens are exploring partnerships in Central Asia to secure raw materials and tap into a growing consumer market of over 75 million people. Furthermore, Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan possess significant hydrocarbon reserves that Europe views as potential long-term alternatives to Russian gas, provided the infrastructure for trans-Caspian pipelines can be realized despite environmental and geopolitical objections from Moscow.
Central Asia's Geopolitical Balancing Act
For the Central Asian republics, the Berlin summit offers vital diplomatic leverage and access to European green technology, allowing them to pursue a "multi-vector" foreign policy. Since the outbreak of the war in Ukraine and the subsequent Western sanctions on Moscow, the five nations have been forced to carefully navigate their economic dependencies. While Russia remains a crucial security partner and labor market destination, and China dominates regional infrastructure through the Belt and Road Initiative, Central Asian leaders are actively courting European capital to balance these overwhelming influences.
The leaders of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, in particular, have positioned themselves as reliable, reform-minded partners willing to adhere to international environmental and governance standards in exchange for Western investment. However, the region remains deeply entangled with the Russian economy, making strict compliance with Western secondary sanctions a constant diplomatic tightrope.
Translating Declarations into Supply Chains
While the Berlin summit underscores Central Asia's transformation from a post-Soviet periphery into a vital geopolitical pivot, translating high-level declarations into concrete, sanction-compliant supply chains remains a complex logistical challenge. The region's landlocked geography, coupled with aging Soviet-era infrastructure and complex border disputes, requires massive, long-term capital commitments that European private markets have historically been hesitant to provide without heavy state guarantees.
Furthermore, the environmental impact of mining critical minerals in the ecologically fragile regions of the Tian Shan mountains and the Aral Sea basin will be a point of contention with European civil society groups. The success of the Z5+1 format will ultimately be measured not by the diplomatic communiqués issued in Berlin, but by the speed at which German and Central Asian consortiums can finance and build the physical infrastructure required to move critical minerals from the steppe to European factories.
