articles.title: Fueling both sides? South Korea ships 150,000T fuel to Russia while funding Ukraine - The Times of India
articles.summary: Fueling both sides? South Korea ships 150,000T fuel to Russia while funding Ukraine  The Times of India
articles.full_text:
South Korea is backing Ukraine, but its fuel tankers are sailing in the opposite direction — towards Russia.
In July and August, more than 176,000 tonnes of fuel, mainly diesel, was shipped from South Korea to Russia as Moscow turned to imports to make up for falling domestic fuel production.
The fuel was loaded at several South Korean ports and carried to Russia’s far east in 14 voyages by seven tankers, according to an analysis of port records and ship-tracking data by The Guardian. Three of the vessels were under UK and European Union sanctions.
One sanctioned tanker received about 26,000 tonnes of fuel from another vessel in a ship-to-ship transfer in South Korean waters. Such transfers can make cargo origins harder to trace and allow ships to avoid port terminals.
Three sanctioned tankers sail to Russia
The largest carrier was the sanctioned Layla, which made two trips from Ulsan in south-eastern South Korea to Vladivostok on 19 July and 10 August, carrying 57,000 tonnes of diesel in total.
On its first trip, Layla told South Korean authorities it was heading to Vladivostok. On the second, it declared Niigata in Japan as its destination before sailing to Vladivostok.
The Russian-flagged Astoria, also under Australian sanctions, loaded nearly 11,000 tonnes of fuel at Ulsan on 1 August. 
It declared Japan as its destination before sailing to Vladivostok.
The third sanctioned tanker, Chongchon, did not berth at a port. Instead, it took on about 26,000 tonnes of fuel from the unsanctioned Celeste I at an anchorage off Yeosu in southern South Korea in early August. It then sailed to Vladivostok after declaring Singapore as its destination.
The owners and managers of the four tankers did not respond to requests for comment. South Korean port records do not show who owned or sold the fuel.
Russia turns to import fuel
The shipments come as Ukrainian drone strikes disrupt Russia’s oil-refining capacity.
The International Energy Agency said Russian refinery throughput fell in June to its lowest level in more than 20 years. Diesel production was nearly 30% lower than a year earlier.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, the HUR, has said Moscow has been forced to import fuel products to feed the “Russian war machine”.
Russia imported 368,000 tonnes of oil products by sea in August, according to Kpler data analysed by CREA. That was more than seven times the previous month and the highest monthly total since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
South Korea supplied 112,000 tonnes, or 31%, of the total, second only to India.
Kpler data showed that buyers included Rosneft, Russia’s state-controlled oil company, which is under UK, US, EU and Australian sanctions. NNK, a Russian oil group, was also among the buyers. Its owner, Eduard Khudainatov, and NNK-Oil are under UK sanctions.
South Korea balances Ukraine support with Russia ties
The fuel trade comes despite South Korea’s support for Ukraine. Seoul has provided humanitarian aid and non-lethal military supplies, including helmets, body armour and demining vehicles. In 2023, it pledged $2.3bn in support, most of it in loans.
President Lee Jae Myung also pledged $100m for Ukraine’s reconstruction at a Nato summit in Turkey.
But Seoul has also sought to maintain ties with Russia. Throughout the war, it has ruled out sending weapons directly to Ukraine, in line with its policy of not supplying lethal arms to countries at war.
Moscow has also shown interest in restoring relations with South Korea, including trade ties.
The fuel shipments involve vessels sanctioned by some of South Korea’s western partners but do not appear to breach South Korean law. Seoul’s measures against Russia mainly focus on export controls covering goods such as industrial machinery, electronics and vehicles.
The shipments come as relations between Seoul and Kyiv face strain over the transfer of two North Korean prisoners of war to South Korea, which Seoul has said was meant to remain secret.
Seoul defends its export controls
Fuel loadings at South Korean ports began to rise sharply in July, around the time Lee pledged $100m for Ukraine’s reconstruction.
A 2025 trade association survey found that nearly 80% of South Korean companies that had stopped exporting to Russia since the war began were open to restarting trade.
In March, South Korea capped exports of certain fuels and imported Russian naphtha under a US sanctions waiver after the war with Iran shut the Strait of Hormuz.
On 1 October, the UK temporarily exempted South Korea’s existing gas contracts from a ban on maritime services for Russian LNG, which will take effect in January 2027.
South Korea’s foreign ministry did not directly address the shipments or the sanctioned tankers. In a statement, it said that as “a responsible member of the international community, the government supports, and is actively taking part in, international efforts to help end the war in Ukraine and bring about a peaceful recovery.”
The ministry said that it had expanded export controls on Russia under the Foreign Trade Act “beyond strategic items to 1,402 non-strategic items with a high potential for diversion to military use” and was “strictly enforcing” them.
The government “continues to monitor the implementation of its export controls on Russia and, where necessary, takes action in accordance with the relevant laws and regulations,” the ministry said.

articles.full_text:
Uzbekistan’s Economic Reforms and Their Impact on Foreign Investment and Growth
By Felix Light and Karin Strohecker
Overview of Uzbekistan's Economic Transformation
TASHKENT/LONDON, Oct 6 (Reuters) - When Nika Kurdiani began to plot London-listed Georgian lender TBC Bank's expansion into Uzbekistan around 2018, he had to bring plastic bags full of banknotes to pay restaurant bills.
The country of nearly 40 million people — Central Asia's most populous — had long been largely closed to foreign investment by strict capital controls. Its currency, the sum, was artificially overvalued and credit cards rarely accepted, forcing consumers to carry wads of cash for everyday purchases.
Progress in Financial Modernization
But after almost a decade of economic reform that has helped growth outpace that of most ex-Soviet peers, digital payments are ubiquitous. TBC Uzbekistan, one of few foreign lenders operating in a still mostly state-owned banking sector, is considering an initial public offering (IPO) separate from its Georgian parent.
"Now there is no need whatsoever to carry cash anywhere in the country," Kurdiani, CEO of TBC's Uzbekistan business, told Reuters in an interview at the bank's Tashkent headquarters.
Attracting International Investors
The changes have begun to attract international investors.
In May, Uzbekistan's National Investment Fund, a portfolio of minority stakes in state-owned companies managed by Franklin Templeton, raised $690 million in the London Stock Exchange's biggest IPO since 2021, drawing over $2.8 billion in orders.
"The reforms have been meaningful in our view, and they are much more open towards market practices," said Leonard Kwan, a fixed-income portfolio manager at T. Rowe Price, which is overweight Uzbekistan.
Challenges to Reform Sustainability
But as the government says it will push ahead with further privatisations, investors say the next test is whether business-friendly changes can become embedded in a country where market-oriented policies remain relatively new and their staying power unclear.
"The biggest risk the country has is the sustainability of all those reforms and the consistency of their implementation," said Kurdiani.
Economic Growth and Investment Trends
Fast-Growing Economy
FAST-GROWING
Policies launched since President Shavkat Mirziyoyev took office in 2016 have opened up a country that had largely shunned the outside world following independence in 1991.
Capital controls have been lifted, the currency has been floated and visa rules eased for most Western visitors.
"The country was effectively closed. It was closed to investors, to visitors," Laziz Kudratov, Uzbekistan's investment minister, told Reuters.
The reforms "led foreign investors, who are seeking new markets and new growth opportunities, to turn their attention to Uzbekistan and begin actively expanding their operations here," Kudratov said.
The Uzbek economy has grown by an average of around 6% over the last five years, faster than most of its neighbours.
Foreign direct investment rose to $4.4 billion in 2025 from $2.3 billion in 2021, according to World Bank and United Nations data, although it remains relatively modest as a share of gross domestic product.
State-Owned Enterprises and IPO Prospects
State-owned enterprises still dominate key sectors like banking, energy and mining. Their assets amounted to more than 100% of GDP at end-2024 according to the International Monetary Fund — a very large footprint by international standards.
Some — including the national gold and uranium miners — have said they may explore London listings following May's National Investment Fund IPO, without giving specific timelines.
Fintech group Uzum, supermarket Korzinka and Uzbekistan Airways have also said they might pursue foreign IPOs.
Institutional and Bureaucratic Challenges
Bureaucratic Inertia
BUREAUCRATIC INERTIA
Investors see little risk of a return to the isolationist policies of the past. Instead, many are focused on whether reforms can become institutionalised and continue despite resistance from parts of the bureaucracy.
"There is strong commitment to reform and economic liberalisation at the highest levels in Uzbekistan," said Dakota Irvin, an analyst at London-based consultancy Lamplighter.
"But there are issues with implementation. Uzbekistan's state bureaucracy remains conservative and averse to change, and there are signs that some investors are experiencing delays or difficulty in getting projects off the ground."
Legal and Political Considerations
Ratings agency Moody's said in June that any slowdown in reforms was among factors that could put pressure on Uzbekistan's credit rating.
Irvin said much of the privatisation programme has been driven through presidential decrees rather than a developed legislative framework, leaving some investors concerned about legal protections and the long-term durability of reforms.
Political authority remains concentrated around Mirziyoyev, with his daughter, Saida — who has served as the public face of the reform agenda — heading the presidential administration and overseeing a special economic zone launched in Tashkent this year.
Workforce and Demographic Factors
Business leaders also cite a shortage of skilled workers, saying the education system is struggling to keep pace with private-sector demand despite the country's youthful population. Even so, executives argue that a generation that has known only a more open Uzbekistan makes any return to the past increasingly unlikely.
"There is a line after which there is a point of no return," said TBC Uzbekistan's Kurdiani. "I think Uzbekistan crossed that line already."
(Editing by Catherine Evans)

President Shavkat Mirziyoyev has repeatedly invited Trump to visit Uzbekistan at a time convenient for the U.S. president. Trump thanked Mirziyoyev for the invitation.
In February this year, Mirziyoyev travelled to Washington at Trump’s invitation to attend the first meeting of the Peace Council. Trump has also invited the Uzbek president to the next meeting of the Peace Council and the G20 summit in Miami.
